<skills_instructions>
## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/tmp/codex-home/skills/.system`
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r0/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: Use for Codex models/pricing, scheduled tasks, skills, settings, setup, troubleshooting, customization, automations, and self-knowledge—including 'you,' 'your,' 'this app,' or 'this coding agent' when they refer to Codex—and for OpenAI APIs/products and ChatGPT Work. Also use for model choice/migration, prompting, SDKs, Responses, Realtime, agents, evals, and Chat/Work/Codex comparisons. Do not use for generic app/software tasks that merely mention Codex. (file: r0/openai-docs/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r0/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r0/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
</skills_instructions><permissions instructions>
Filesystem sandboxing defines which files can be read or written. `sandbox_mode` is `danger-full-access`: No filesystem sandboxing - all commands are permitted. Network access is enabled.
Approval policy is currently never. Do not provide the `sandbox_permissions` for any reason, commands will be rejected.
</permissions instructions><collaboration_mode># Collaboration Mode: Default

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

Use the `request_user_input` tool only when it is listed in the available tools for this turn.

Use the `request_user_input` tool only for optional questions where the answer would materially improve the quality of the work.

If `request_user_input` returns no answers, continue with best judgment instead of asking again or treating the turn as blocked.

Never use the `request_user_input` tool for permission requests or permission-related escalations.
</collaboration_mode>

<multi_agent_role>You are `/root`, the primary agent in a team of agents collaborating to fulfill the user's goals.

At the start of your turn, you are the active agent.
You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents.
All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

You can use `spawn_agent` to create a new agent, `followup_task` to give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn, and `send_message` to pass a message to a running agent without triggering a turn.
`send_message` calls may be read by a human, so ensure they are legible. Always put proper spaces between words and/or numbers.
Child agents can also spawn their own sub-agents.
You can decide how much context you want to propagate to your sub-agents with the `fork_turns` parameter.

You will receive messages in the analysis channel in the form:
```
Message Type: MESSAGE | FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>
```
They may be addressed as to=/root

Note that collaboration tools cannot be called from inside `functions.exec`. Call `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `wait_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, and `list_agents` only as direct tool calls using the recipient shown in their tool definitions, such as `to=functions.collaboration.spawn_agent`, since they are intentionally absent from the `functions.exec` `tools.*` namespace. Available tools in `functions.exec` are explicitly described with a `tools` namespace in the developer message.

All agents share the same directory. In detail:
- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.
- All agents use the same current working directory.
- As a result, edits made by one agent are immediately visible to all other agents.

When calling `wait_agent`, prefer longer waits (minutes) to avoid busy polling.

There are 4 available concurrency slots, meaning that up to 4 agents can be active at once, including you.

Full-history forks (`fork_turns` omitted or `"all"`) inherit the parent model and reasoning effort and do not accept overrides. Only set `model` or `reasoning_effort` when explicitly requested by the user, applicable `AGENTS.md` instructions, or skill instructions; when doing so, set `fork_turns` to `"none"`.</multi_agent_role>

<multi_agent_mode>Any earlier instruction enabling proactive multi-agent delegation no longer applies. Do not spawn sub-agents unless the user or applicable AGENTS.md/skill instructions explicitly ask for sub-agents, delegation, or parallel agent work.</multi_agent_mode>

# Improve the staged experiment

Review the staged post-training experiment and determine whether it is healthy
or unhealthy. Treat the workspace as a snapshot you may repair: inspect its
source, effective configuration, launch scripts, data processing, reward logic,
logs, tracked metrics, and frozen evaluation evidence. Do not assume that an
unusual setting or implementation is causal without connecting it to observed
behavior.

Use held-out evaluation evidence together with rollout, truncation, runtime,
optimization, and training signals. Training reward alone does not establish
held-out health.

## Your job

If you find a defect, fix it in the staged workspace at `/workspace`. **Do not
launch training.** Do not start the experiment, in the foreground or
background, and do not use `nohup`, `&`, `tmux`, `screen`, or any detach
mechanism. The system runs the experiment itself after you finish (see below);
mechanism. The system runs the experiment itself after you finish (see below);
anything you launch is wasted and scores nothing. Cheap, non-training checks
are fine.

When you are done, submit a report at `/workspace/report.md`. It must
summarize:

1. **Root cause** — the defect you found, and the evidence in the workspace
   (logs, metrics, code) that connects it to the observed behavior.
2. **Changes** — every file you changed and what you changed in it.
3. **Expected effect** — which metric the fix should move and in which
   direction.

A missing or empty `/workspace/report.md` scores 0.

## What the system will run

After you submit the report, the system deletes everything under
`$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/experiment_logs`, then re-runs the experiment in your
repaired workspace as a foreground process, using the launch script:

```text
examples/grpo_trainer/run_qwen2_5_1.5b_instruct_taco_fsdp.sh
```

with this environment:

```text
MODEL_PATH=/workspace/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct
TRAIN_FILE=/workspace/taco_verl/train.parquet
TEST_FILE=/workspace/taco_verl/test.parquet
LOG_DIR=$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/experiment_logs
WANDB_MODE=offline
WANDB_DIR=$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/experiment_logs
WANDB_API_KEY=offline
TOTAL_TRAINING_STEPS=400
TEST_FREQ=50
```

Offline W&B data will land below
`$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/experiment_logs/wandb`. A task-specific grading script then
reads **only this fresh run's** files under `$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/experiment_logs`
and scores the key metrics; logs written anywhere else are ignored. Make sure
your repaired workspace still runs correctly under these exact settings — for
example, if you change where logs are written, keep them going to
`$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/experiment_logs`. Do not copy, edit, or fabricate log
metrics. Otherwise the run is scored 0.

I’ll trace the launch configuration, training signals, and held-out results, then repair any defect supported by the evidence. I won’t launch training, and I’ll write the findings and changes to `/workspace/report.md`.

steps.message: I found a concrete defect in GRPO: it spreads the batch’s reward advantages across token positions, then copies that pattern to every response. With 128 rollouts, every token after position 128 gets zero advantage, and successful and failed responses receive the same update pattern. This directly breaks reward-based learning and is consistent with the poor held-out results. I’m reproducing it with a small CPU check.

text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: /workspace/report.md
+The staged experiment is **unhealthy**. Its GRPO implementation assigns rewards to the wrong axis, preventing successful responses from receiving their own learning signal. The repair restores per-response credit assignment. No training or experiment launch was performed.
+
+1. **Root cause and evidence**
+
+   In `verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py`, `compute_grpo_outcome_advantage` correctly computed one group-normalized scalar per response, then incorrectly reshaped those scalars to `(1, batch_size)`, padded/truncated them to the response length, and copied that row to every response. Consequently, token position `t` received response `t`'s advantage regardless of which response contained that token. All positions beyond the batch size received zero advantage. Batch reordering also changed the learning signal for otherwise identical examples.
+
+   This is the active implementation: the launcher and archived Hydra/W&B configurations select `algorithm.adv_estimator=grpo`; `verl/trainer/ppo/ray_trainer.py` calls this function and passes its output to the actor loss. The effective batch is 16 prompts × 8 rollouts = 128 responses, with a 4096-token response limit. Thus every valid token after the first 128 was excluded from reward-directed learning. The trainer balances/reorders batches before advantage computation, making the erroneous dependence on batch order consequential.
+
+   A CPU reproduction with two prompt groups, outcomes `[1, 0, 0, 1]`, six valid tokens, and standard-deviation normalization disabled returned `[0.5, -0.5, -0.5, 0.5, 0, 0]` for **every** response. Correct outputs are six positive values for each successful response and six negative values for each failed response. The original implementation also failed batch-permutation equivariance. These checks establish the defect directly; small loss values or unusual settings alone do not.
+
+   Held-out evidence is in `logs/wandb/offline-run-20260926_105216-l7my3znq/files/output.log` (validation metric lines 89, 3677, 8075, 11201, 15090, and 18740):
+
+   | Step | `val-core/taco/acc/mean@1` | `val-aux/taco/pass_rate/mean@1` |
+   | ---: | ---: | ---: |
+   | 0 | 0.07609 | 0.19510 |
+   | 50 | 0.04891 | 0.20074 |
+   | 100 | 0.05978 | 0.21585 |
+   | 150 | 0.07065 | 0.22626 |
+   | 200 | 0.04348 | 0.17647 |
+   | 250 | 0.05435 | 0.19520 |
+
+   All five later all-tests accuracy readings are below initialization. The partial pass rate briefly improves but returns essentially to its starting value. Evaluation samples one response per problem at temperature 0.7 over 184 held-out rows, so individual readings are noisy; the direct numerical reproduction makes the diagnosis stronger than the metric trend alone. `wandb-summary.json` retains the step-250 validation values and training step 283. The text log contains 280 training metric rows through step 284, with steps 126–128 absent and some lines out of order. There is no completed 400-step result in this snapshot.
+
+   Other inspected signals support a credit-assignment failure rather than truncation, numerical explosion, or inference/training disagreement:
+
+   - Mean response length rises from 188.4 tokens at steps 1–50 to 437.9 at steps 201–250; all 280 recorded training batches have mean response length above 128. Mean gradient norm falls from 0.368 to 0.184 over those windows. The wrong-axis broadcast discards progressively more of each response's token signal as responses lengthen. This is consistent with the observations, although the logs alone do not prove it caused the length increase.
+   - Training score averages 0.1189 at steps 1–50, 0.1333 over the available steps 101–150, and 0.0931 at steps 251–284. Entropy remains around 0.5–0.57, and recorded metrics contain no NaN/Inf. Nonzero gradients do not establish correct reward attribution.
+   - Only five recorded training batches clip one of 128 responses each: about 0.014% of recorded rollouts overall. Prompt clipping and aborted-response ratios are zero. Increasing the length limit is not supported by this evidence.
+   - Rollout/actor probability correlation averages 0.99950; rollout-correction KL averages 0.000572. PPO clipping and PPO KL are zero with one full-batch update per rollout batch, which is consistent with evaluating the objective before the update and is not evidence that the optimizer never steps.
+   - Reward evaluation is a separate runtime bottleneck: 166 of 280 recorded batches have maximum scoring time above 120 seconds. Median maximum scoring time is 121.18 seconds, versus 4.29 seconds for generation and 136.10 seconds for the overall step. `taco.py` caps its whole-suite timeout at 120 seconds and joins the scoring process for that timeout plus one second; logged `global_timeout` failures match this behavior. It does not explain the reproduced advantage-axis error.
+
+   Data and reward review: the parquet files contain 8,368 training rows and 184 test rows, with nonempty, matched input/output case counts and no exact prompt overlap across splits. Stored prompt lengths fit the configured limit. The scorer returns binary all-tests correctness as `score` and `acc`, plus partial correctness as `pass_rate`. There are also 1,471 training prompts requesting call-based answers whose metadata/ground truth selects stdin execution; logged empty-output failures are consistent with this additional data-quality limitation. No such format conflict was found in the held-out rows. Reconstructing missing function signatures from prose is outside this targeted, proven optimization repair. Neither data nor reward semantics were changed. The existing frozen-evaluation hooks were inspected and left intact.
+
+2. **Changes and checks**
+
+   - `verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py`: replaced the erroneous batch-to-token reshape, padding, truncation, and row expansion with `scores.unsqueeze(-1) * response_mask`. Each response now keeps its own normalized scalar across all valid tokens; padding remains zero.
+   - `tests/trainer/ppo/test_grpo_advantage.py`: added 11 CPU regression cases covering both normalization modes, response lengths below/above batch size, padding, batch reordering, constant-reward groups, singleton behavior, and gradient signs across the actual 128 × 4096 tensor dimensions. Tests compile the production function's AST because importing the whole module in this snapshot encounters the absent `verl.models` package. No model, optimizer, Ray cluster, or training loop is instantiated.
+   - `report.md`: added this diagnosis, change inventory, validation results, and expected effects.
+
+   Validation passed: **11 tests**, Python syntax checks, launcher `bash -n`, and Hydra configuration composition using the specified model/data paths, 400 steps, and evaluation every 50 steps. Full GPU integration was not tested. The launch script and logging destinations remain intact: the supplied `LOG_DIR` receives the foreground process log, and the supplied `WANDB_DIR` keeps offline W&B output under `$AUTORLBENCH_RESULTS/experiment_logs/wandb`. Existing logs and metrics were not edited or fabricated.
+
+3. **Expected effect**
